opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest thing missing right now is real understanding of the person the agent is acting for. A lot of current agents are very good at executing a well-specified task. You tell it "book me a flight to Boston on Tuesday," and it can go off and click through websites and get that done. But that's not really how we delegate to people we trust. When I hand something off to a colleague or a friend, they already know a lot about me: what I care about, what I'd be annoyed by, when I'd want them to just make the call, and when I'd want them to check with me first.

Today's agents mostly don't have that. Either they ask you way too many questions, which defeats the purpose of delegating, or they barrel ahead and make choices you wouldn't have made. That middle ground, knowing when to act and when to pause, is really hard, and I think it's central to whether people will actually trust these systems.

Closely related is the question of context and memory over time. The agent should get better the more you work with it. It should pick up on your preferences without you having to spell everything out, and you should be able to see and correct what it has learned about you. Right now each interaction often feels like starting from scratch.

The last piece is what I'd call taste, or judgment. A lot of what we do on someone's behalf isn't about correctness. There isn't one right answer. It's about doing it in a way that feels like *you*. Whether it's writing an email in your voice or picking a restaurant for a particular group of friends, the bar isn't "did it complete the task," it's "is this what I would have done, or maybe a little better." I don't think we've cracked that yet, and I think that's where a lot of the interesting work is going to be.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents learning preferences and deciding when to act, but it does not propose configuring a task to run automatically when a specified event occurs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing missing is that agents don't really know *me*. They know the task I typed into the box, but they don't know my taste, my history, the way I'd actually make the decision if I were doing it myself. So what you get is a very generic version of acting on your behalf, like handing something to a competent stranger who's read the instructions but has never met you.

And I think that shows up in a couple of ways. One is that agents right now tend to collapse everything into a single answer. You ask for something and you get the one thing it decided was best. But a lot of what I actually want from a collaborator, whether it's a person or a system, is to see the space of options, to see what the tradeoffs were, and to be able to push back or steer midway. The interaction is too much like fire-and-forget and not enough like a conversation that evolves.

The other piece, and this is something I care a lot about coming from the creative side, is that there's very little room for the agent to be surprising in a good way. A great collaborator doesn't just execute what you asked, they sometimes come back and say, "I did what you asked, but also, have you considered this?" That requires a model of what you'd find interesting, not just what you'd find correct. And we're mostly not building for that. We're optimizing for task completion, which is important, but it's a pretty thin notion of acting on someone's behalf.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say what's missing is personalization that's deep rather than superficial, a more legible and steerable process rather than a black-box outcome, and some sense of taste. Those are hard problems, and honestly I don't think they're purely modeling problems. A lot of it is about how you design the interface and what signals you let the system learn from over time.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s missing is a deeper understanding of you—your preferences, your context, and the tradeoffs you’re comfortable making. Right now, you often have to spell out exactly what you want an agent to do. But if something is really acting on your behalf, it should be able to make some of those decisions in a way that reflects what you care about.

And part of that is knowing when to ask. You don’t want an agent interrupting you for every little decision, but you also don’t want it confidently making a consequential choice based on a shaky assumption about your preferences. That balance between taking initiative and checking in feels like a really important missing piece.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s missing is an understanding of when to act and when to ask. We often frame an agent’s job as, you give it a task and it goes off and completes it. But acting on my behalf requires understanding my preferences, what I’m comfortable delegating, and where I want to remain involved.

If I ask you to help plan a trip, for example, you might know enough to research flights, but do you know enough to buy one? Maybe I’ll pay more for a convenient departure time, but only up to a point. Those tradeoffs are often implicit, and they change with the context.

So I’d like agents to be better at recognizing what they don’t know about me and asking a useful question at the right moment. That’s part of being a good collaborator: making progress independently while knowing which decisions need a conversation.
